newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: COMPANY COLUMN-Eco-tourism firm reaps jungle money.
newsitem.headline: COMPANY COLUMN-Eco-tourism firm reaps jungle money.

text.p: Anthony Wong says he has climbed Southeast Asia's tallest peak, Mount Kinabalu, 36 times.
He did this over a six-year period starting from 1976, when he was practically broke.
For Wong, 41, managing director of Malaysian eco-tourism operators Asian Overland Services Sdn Bhd, climbing mountains is not just a form of spiritual healing, it's part of his livelihood.
"I left school in 1975, but I could not go to university because my family was very poor. I have always worked, even while studying. You become very disciplined," said Wong.
Asian Overland was one of the first companies in Southeast Asia to offer package tours into the heart of Malaysia's rainforests, Wong said.

The rainforests of Borneo, which contain Malaysia's two eastern states of Sabah and Sarawak, are among the last of their type in the world. Scientists say many species of flora and fauna in those forests have yet to be discovered and catalogued.
The company began operations in 1976, specialising in arranging tours for students travelling on shoe-string budgets. Wong was 19.
"I had been running trips to Sabah and Sarawak since 1974. I was among the first to be doing such tours."
Today, Wong is regarded as an expert on how to make eco-tourism work in Malaysia. His insights are even sought by local universities.
"Because we were the pioneers in this field we were asked to lecture as to how... to make eco-tourism work," he said.
And his company has grown with the popularity of the industry. Asian Overland had a turnover of around 18 million ringgit ($7.2 million) in 1996, and employs nearly 80 people.
Originally more famed for its beaches, Malaysia over the past few years has been opening up its lush forests to the adventure travel and eco-tourism industry.

Among the more popular offerings from the industry are chalets equipped for observing wildlife at the Taman Negara national forest, an orangutan rehabilitation centre in the Borneo state of Sabah that reintroduces tamed apes into the jungle, the famed Mulu limestone caves in Sarawak, white water rafting and homestays on old plantations.
Malaysia aims to attract 12.5 million visitors by the year 2000 against around 7.5 million in 1996. The country earned around 8 billion ringgit ($3.2 billion) from tourism last year.
The pursuit of ringgit drives most companies in the eco-tourism business but Wong says his goal is to educate.
"Going into the jungle teaches you to have a balanced lifestyle. It recharges your battery, it makes you look outside-in."
"My philosophy is not to disrupt the local lifestyles."

In 1990, Wong began taking tourists into the relatively isolated villages of Sarawak. He had to create much of the basic infrastructure needed to develop the villages to cater to Western travellers. Six months were spent educating the villagers on how to cope with the tourists they would meet. Won then took the villagers to luxury hotels in the state capital to show them some of the amenities that would be necessary for the tourists.
Over the six years of the project, the average income of each villager rose from around 35 ringgit per month to 140 ringgit per month, he said.

But a timber company bought the tree-felling rights in the area from the villagers. Logging cleared the patch of forest that had been home to 800 people, putting an end to Wong's venture in that village.
Now Asian Overland has begun taking stressed-out workers from large city corporations to its custom-built Jungle Lodge, around an hour's drive outside the capital Kuala Lumpur.
Office-bound executives used to being by chauffeur-driven face such novel experiences as lugging their own tents up hills.
($1=2.5 ringgit)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
